sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: An upper level ridge over the area will shift inland today. Areas of fog will be the main concern across western Washington this morning. The next disturbance will move into the region this afternoon and will bring light lowland rain and mountain snow to the area. The pattern becomes more active next week as a series of systems brings widespread precipitation, gusty winds, and the increasing potential for coastal flooding.

sections.title: Short term (today through Monday)
paragraphs: An upper level ridge over the area this morning will push inland today, making way for the next system to move into the region by this afternoon and evening. Conditions are cool out there again this morning, with temperatures mainly trending in the upper 20s to mid 30s as of 1AM/09Z. Areas of fog have also redeveloped across the area again overnight, and with temperatures near freezing, can expect to see a few areas of freezing fog across the region again this morning.

An upper level low will then drop southward from the NE Pacific today and position itself offshore through Sunday. This system will bring the next round of light rain to the lowlands and light snow to the mountains. Rain will approach the coast by this afternoon and will then gradually push inland into the interior by this evening. Overall rainfall amounts will remain light through Sunday, with only a tenth to a quarter of an inch of rain expected along the coast and a few hundredths of an inch for the interior - with many spots remaining dry. Snow levels will hover between 2000-3000 ft, so will see some light snow accumulations (less than half an inch) at the Cascade passes. Afternoon high temperatures today and Sunday will be in the mid 40s to low 50s. Lastly, high astronomical tides over the weekend may bring the potential for some minor coastal flooding along the Pacific Coast and the Strait of Juan de Fuca by Sunday.

The low situated offshore will eventually become absorbed into the mean flow on Monday as a broad upper level low drops down into the NE Pacific from the Aleutians. Another round of precipitation will push inland, but will largely remain focused on the Olympic Peninsula. Snow amounts between 4-8 inches will be possible in the Olympics. Afternoon highs will be in mid 40s to low 50s.

sections.title: Long term (Monday night through Friday)
paragraphs: The aforementioned low will then deepen offshore Monday night into Tuesday and will bring a more active pattern to western Washington as the system swings a number of disturbances across the region. Expect multiple rounds of widespread lowland rain, mountain snow, and gusty winds starting Tuesday and persisting through the second half of the week. The system moving across the area on Tuesday will also bring another round of high surf to the coast. Additionally, high astronomical tides combined with the weather impacts from these systems, will increase the threat for coastal flooding - most notably along the Pacific Coast during high surf.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Weak high pressure will begin to move out of the terminals today as an occluded front slows over water as it approaches the coastline. A column of low-end MVFR stratus has formed and work its way north through the Puget Sound this morning. Cameras however are showing fog and mist developing underneath the stratus layer, with much of it remaining localized over areas of water, and any low-lying areas or valleys. High cloud coverage does not arrive until early this afternoon, so this will likely keep lower ceilings/visibilities around through the morning - as late as 18Z. Showers with the front will arrive along the coast shortly after 18Z, and push inland towards 00Z. Overnight, as the showers push through ceilings will gradually lower to either a low-end VFR or MVFR level early Sunday morning, with the lowest ceilings in the south interior. Showers will continue Sunday with ceilings improving to VFR late in the morning. Winds will be out of the south/southeast 5-10 kt with a few gusts to 20 kt.

KSEA...Low MVFR ceilings likely to hang around the terminal through 18Z as high clouds arrive with the front. Cameras are picking up on lower areas of visibilities underneath the stratus near the terminal, particularly to the northeast (some patches of fog). VFR is expected after 18Z this afternoon with MVFR becoming likely post- showers overnight (as early as 09Z). Winds: southeast 5-10 kt with a few gusts to 20 kt later in the afternoon.
HPR

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A front will slow to a near stall over the coastal waters this weekend, with high pressure moving out. Couple areas of fog may linger in the interior waters this morning. The front will bring some showers (no thunder expected through the weekend). Winds remain on track to increase with the frontal system this afternoon today into Sunday. This system will primarily affect the coastal waters, and the east Strait of Juan de Fuca, with winds of 20-30 kt today. The northwest coastal water zone does still have the best chance of a few gale gusts this afternoon. The coastal system will deepen and keep winds gusty on Sunday and into Monday out of the southeast. A couple strong system remains on track to impact the waters Monday into Tuesday, and Wednesday. PRobabilities remain high for gale gusts in the coastal waters, and a portion of the east Strait of Juan de Fuca. There remains a 20-40% chance of wind gusts reaching storm force criteria with of the next week systems.
Seas will build from 6 to 8 to 8 to 12 ft today, and continue to build on Monday up to 16 to 20 ft, before decreasing back to 10 to 14 ft by the end of next week.
HPR

sections.title: Hydrology
paragraphs: Wetter systems moving into the region next week will start to bring some rises to area rivers. At this time, no widespread river flooding is expected, however the Skokomish River will likely cross into flood stage late in the week.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: Dry weather quickly gives way today as an active, wet Pacific pattern takes hold across northwest Oregon and southwest Washington, bringing multiple rounds of rain, mountain snow, and breezy winds through next week. A series of frontal systems will keep conditions unsettled through Thanksgiving Day and into late week. Forecast models indicate a low-probability risk for a stronger low pressure system to track closer to the coast late next week, which could introduce higher wind and heavy rain impacts.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Dry weather quickly gives way today as an active, wet Pacific pattern takes hold across northwest Oregon and southwest Washington, bringing multiple rounds of rain, mountain snow, and breezy winds through next week. A series of frontal systems will keep conditions unsettled through Thanksgiving Day and into late week. Forecast models indicate a low-probability risk for a stronger low pressure system to track closer to the coast late next week, which could introduce higher wind and heavy rain impacts.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Friday...Quiet and dry weather lingering across the region early today will rapidly deteriorate as a deep upper-level trough off the Pacific brings an active and wet pattern for the upcoming week. The first frontal system will push onshore this morning, bringing coastal rain showers by late this morning and spreading inland through this afternoon. This initial weekend system will keep snow levels down around 2500 to 3500 feet, but with limited moisture staying mostly offshore, snowfall accumulations at Cascade pass levels will remain light, generally under 2 inches for most spots through Sunday. Travelers across the Cascades should still anticipate occasional slick roads during heavier showers.

The weather pattern turns progressively wetter and more impactful heading into early next week as a stronger low pressure system deepens off the Pacific. A robust frontal passage from late Monday through Wednesday will tap into Pacific moisture, featuring integrated water vapor transport values peaking around 500 to 650 kg/(m s). During this 48-hour surge, latest forecast guidance points to a 60-80% probability for a least 1 inch of rain along the coast, 40-70% across the Cascades, and 30-50% for the inland valleys, with the highest chances focused north of the Columbia River. Localized ponding of water in poor drainage and low-lying areas remains possible during periods of heavier rain, though significant river flooding is not currently anticipated.

In addition to widespread lowland rainfall and mountain snow, coastal communities and headlands will experience periods of gusty winds as frontal boundaries sweep onshore. Tuesday brings the initial notable wind threat along the beaches and immediate coast, where forecast models indicate a 40-60% chance of peak wind gusts reaching 45 mph or higher, and a 5-20% chance of gusts exceeding 55 mph. Breezy conditions will also extend inland into the lower Columbia River Valley and portions of the Portland metro area at times, though speeds will be notably lower than coastal exposures.

Before the active frontal weather arrives in full force, near- term sensible weather will feature typical late-autumn conditions. Morning valley fog and patchy frost will develop where clearing skies allow overnight lows to drop into the low to mid 30s across the Willamette Valley, I-5 corridor, and Portland metro area. Afternoon temperatures will recover into the mid to upper 40s in the lowlands and 30s in the higher terrain today before cloud cover thickens and moderates overnight lows upward through the middle of next week.

Looking toward Thanksgiving Day and next Friday, forecast model clusters diverge regarding the exact evolution of subsequent Pacific systems. The majority of ensemble members favor continued unsettled weather with frequent frontal passages bringing additional rounds of rain and breezy winds right through the holiday. However, a minority cluster, representing that low-probability 15-30% alternative, hints at a sharper, more amplified low pressure system tracking closer to the coast, which would elevate the threat for stronger wind gusts and heavier precipitation amounts. Travelers with holiday plans should monitor later forecasts as details surrounding late-week storm tracks become clearer.  ~12

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 12Z Sunday...High pressure continues to maintain calm winds and favorable conditions for fog/stratus development within the Willamette Valley. As of 11Z Sat, widespread fog has expanded over most of the airspace, resulting in LIFR conditions at nearly every inland terminal. Expect these deteriorated conditions to improve to VFR around 17-19Z Sat as a frontal boundary moves through the airspace and improves mixing. Expect light rain showers to arrive at all terminals at that time. Expect heavier/persistent showers heading into tonight, around 04Z Sun. Winds will generally remain around 5-10 kt, southerly in the central/southern Willamette Valley and southeasterly around KPDX and vicinity terminals. Coastal terminals will see southeasterly winds around 10-15 kt with gusts around 20-25 kt through most of the TAF period.

sections.title: Kpdx and approaches
paragraphs: Current LIFR fog will improve to VFR around 18Z as a frontal boundary moves through and promotes mixing. Expect light rain showers to arrive around that time. Heavier and/or more persistent rain showers will begin tonight, around 04Z Sun. Light winds this morning will increase to 5-10 kt out of the southeast from this afternoon to the end of the TAF period.  ~12

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: The next frontal system arrives this morning, increasing southerly winds with gusts up to 30 kt. Small Craft Advisories are in effect through early Sunday morning. For the outer waters beyond 10-20 NM offshore, isolated gale force wind gusts up to 35 kt are possible. Guidance does not suggest frequent or widespread enough gales to warrant a Gale Warning. High confidence (70-90% chance) for seas building to 8-10 ft on Saturday, and 12-14 ft by Sunday. With the possibility of seas reaching 14-15 ft on Sunday with a period of 13-14 seconds, a Hazardous Seas Watch has been issued from 4 AM to 7 PM Sunday for the outer waters south of Cape Falcon.

Active weather continues next week as a series of systems impacts the waters. There is potential for storm force wind gusts early next week, with a 20-50% chance for at least isolated wind gusts exceeding 48 kt across the outer waters beyond 10 NM offshore. In addition, seas will also build into the mid to upper teens, with a 20-40% chance of exceeding 20 ft on Tuesday for areas beyond 30 NM offshore. For the Columbia River Bar, chances for seas exceeding 20 ft are currently around 5-15%.

Long period swells will also result in a moderate threat for sneaker waves through this weekend into Monday, then becoming a high threat beginning Tuesday. Those visiting the coast should use extra precaution when in or near the water. ~12/10
